items.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022
items.q: The interviewee discusses a quote by Kurt Vonnegut mentioning Mozart, but the interviewee does not mention any personal interaction, relationship, or specific knowledge of Mozart himself, only agreeing with the broader cultural statement.

ctx.x: Yeah. That’s nice of you. The blues, it’s — the blues is it’s an expression of your life experience. And that’s really as simple as I could put it. It’s an expression. Now you could put that in any genre or whatever, but since we’re talking about blues it’s an expression of your life experience. And it can pinpoint the joy, the humility, or even some sadness that you may be experiencing or have experienced that’s made a mark on you, it touches — it reflects your spirit in the purest sense. It really does. Because…

Well said. I wanted to share something I read recently and this is the first opportunity I’ve had to share it. This is from Kurt Vonnegut from his last book, A Man Without a Country and I’m only slightly paraphrasing here. Kurt said “I really like Strauss and Mozart and all that, but the priceless gift that African-Americans gave the whole world was a gift so great that it is now almost the only reason many foreigners still like us. All pop music today: jazz, swing, bebop, Elvis Presley, the Beatles, the Stones,…

Yeah. It’s the American experience. The blues is the American experience. Now blues didn’t originate in America. Blues came over from Africa. Okay? I don’t know if you’ve had the opportunity or experience to hear some of the, you know, some of the music in Africa that depicts that sound, but it’s there man. I’ve heard it. And the way it developed here is uniqueness. That’s our culture you know. That’s American culture. And I agree with what he said, this is something that has permeated and touched the rest of the…
